segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello. This is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Neil.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And I'm Georgie.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: So, Georgie, I'd like to know if you have any brothers or sisters and if you get on well with them.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Yes, I do. I have a sister and we get on very well. We didn't used to, but now that we're adults we get on well.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, in this programme we'll be discussing one of the closest relationships there is, the connection between sisters.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: We'll hear from three Irish sisters reuniting on a radio show.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And from a psychotherapist on some stereotypes about sisterhood.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Plus, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary too.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And remember, if you want to read along while you listen, you can find the script for this programme on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Yeah, great idea.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Now, whether you have one or not, our history and culture is full of sisters,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: from the fairy tale of Cinderella and her ugly sisters to tennis players, Venus and Serena Williams.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And currently two sisters, Ellie and Rachel Reeves, are senior ministers in the British government.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: So Neil, my question for you is this.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: What is Rachel Reeves' government job?

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Is she A. Home Secretary, B. Foreign Secretary, or C. Chancellor of the Exchequer?

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well I think the answer is C the Chancellor of the Exchequer which is the name for the finance minister in the UK

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: OK Neil we find out if that the correct answer later in the programme

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Nuala McGovern, the presenter of BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour, has two sisters.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: They both live in Ireland, so they're joining me on a video call.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hello, Eileen. Hello, Vera. Welcome to Woman's Hour.

segments.speaker: Vera
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Eileen
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Nuala was born in Dublin and moved to New York, then London,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: to work as a journalist while her two sisters stayed in Ireland.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Here she introduces her older sister, Vera, and younger sister, Eileen,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: for a BBC Radio 4 Women's Hour special about sisterhood.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Nuala was a little worried what her sisters would say about her on the radio,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: so let's listen in and find out.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Eileen, what would you say if you would describe our relationship as sisters?

segments.speaker: Eileen
segments.text: Very connected, I think, and we do get on very well,

segments.speaker: Eileen
segments.text: which I'm proud to say.

segments.speaker: Eileen
segments.text: Yes, exactly.

segments.speaker: Eileen
segments.text: I'm going to put you on the spot, Vera.

segments.speaker: Eileen
segments.text: What word would you use to describe me as a sister?

segments.speaker: Vera
segments.text: I couldn't give you a word,

segments.speaker: Vera
segments.text: but you'd definitely march to your own drum.

segments.speaker: Vera
segments.text: What would that word be?

segments.speaker: Vera
segments.text: Independent.

segments.speaker: Eileen
segments.text: Independent,

segments.speaker: Vera
segments.text: definitely.

segments.speaker: Vera
segments.text: You liked to control the situation.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Eileen thinks she gets on with her sisters.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: To get on with someone means to like them and have a good relationship with them.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Nula puts her older sister on the spot by asking Vera to describe her in one word.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: When you put someone on the spot you make them answer a difficult question then and there sometimes making them embarrassed or uncomfortable

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: But Nula didn need to worry what her sisters would say Vera simply said that Nula marches to her own drum

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: She does things in her own way,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: which may be different from how other people do things.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: It seems Vera, Nula and Eileen have remained close friends as they've grown up,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: but the relationship between older, middle and younger sisters isn't always so harmonious.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Let's listen to BBC Radio 4's Women's Hour special programme

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: as Nuala is joined by psychotherapist Jennifer Gledhill.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Thank you very much to Eileen and Vera.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: What a treat to have a chat with my sisters about sisters.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: I want to bring in Jennifer here who's listening to it all.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Some of the stereotypes around siblings,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: that the eldest sister is bossy, the middle sister is a peacemaker

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: and the little sister is spoiled, that is not applying to our family.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: But I'm wondering, is there any substance to that

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: or why does that even get bandied around?

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: We love giving people labels, don't we?

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: We like to put people into categories

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: and then we can make sense of behaviours.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: But actually, since then, scientists find no proof

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: of being these roles in the families.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Nula discusses stereotypes about siblings,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: a word that means either brother or sister.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: One stereotype is that the older sister is usually bossy.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: She enjoys telling people what to do.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Another stereotype is that the younger sister is spoiled.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: If you describe a child as spoiled you mean they are allowed to do anything they want often with the result that they behave badly

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: What do you think about these stereotypes Georgie Are they true for you and your sister

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: I not sure I agree with these stereotypes because the older sister is meant to be bossy

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: but my younger sister is the bossy one. I don't think I'm bossy at all.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Well, that's interesting. Jennifer did say that there's no scientific proof.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Anyway, it's time now to find out the answer to your question, Georgie.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Yes. And my question was, what is Rachel Reeve's government job? And you guessed she was the

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Chancellor of the Exchequer, which was the correct answer. Well done, Neil.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Hooray!

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: OK. Let's recap the vocabulary we've learned in this programme, starting with the phrasal verb

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: get on with someone, meaning to have a good relationship with them.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: If you put someone on the spot, you cause them embarrassment by forcing them to answer a

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: difficult question at that very moment.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: If you march to your own drum, you do things in your own unique way, regardless of how other people do them.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: A sibling can mean either a brother or sister.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: People who are bossy enjoy telling other people what to do.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: And finally, a spoiled child is allowed to do whatever they want, becoming badly behaved as a result.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but remember to head over to bbclearningenglish.com

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: where you can find loads more fun and helpful resources,

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: including a worksheet and quiz for this programme.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Bye for now.

segments.speaker: Neil
segments.text: Goodbye.
